claims.text: The target materials are high-entropy alloys spanning varying compositions and processing conditions.

The intervention is to incorporate density estimate, mixing enthalpy, mixing entropy, melting-temperature estimate, valence electron concentration, atomic-size difference, and Pauling-electronegativity difference as inputs to machine-learning models.
Incorporating these empirical parameters will improve machine-learning prediction of phases in high-entropy alloys.
Phase distribution and microstructure mediate the effect of the added empirical model inputs.
The empirical parameters improve phase prediction because they encode materials-science principles relevant to phase selection.
The intervention will improve the accuracy of melting-temperature and other melting-property predictions.
The intervention will improve the computational efficiency of melting-temperature and other melting-property predictions.
Current machine-learning models provide a baseline capability for predicting phases in high-entropy alloys.
The hypothesis should remain valid across high-entropy alloys with varying compositions and processing conditions.
Prediction performance is limited by the quality and quantity of training data.
Prediction performance is limited by machine-learning model complexity.
A controlled benchmark should compare machine-learning models with and without the empirical design parameters.
The benchmark should measure accuracy, computational efficiency, and melting temperature.
Failure of the augmented models to improve both accuracy and efficiency for melting-property prediction would falsify the hypothesis.
